name: Arad
title: The King of Arad – Canaanite ruler in the Negev
summary: The king of Arad was a Canaanite ruler who reigned in the Negev region, south of Canaan. As the Israelites approached the promised land, he attacked them and took some captive. After this defeat, Israel made a solemn vow to the Lord: if God gave them victory over the Canaanites, they would devote the cities to complete destruction (cherem) – a practice in which everything was handed over to God as an expression of his sovereignty over war. The Lord heard Israel’s prayer and granted them victory. The Canaanites were defeated and the cities destroyed, and the place received the name Horma ('destruction'). A king of Arad is also mentioned among the defeated kings in Joshua's list of conquests, but it is uncertain whether this refers to the same person or a later ruler over the same area.

keyEvents.title: The King of Arad Attacks Israel
keyEvents.description: The Canaanite king of Arad, who lived in the Negev, heard that the Israelites were approaching on the road to Atharim. He attacked them and took some of them captive.

keyEvents.title: Israel's Vow to the Lord
keyEvents.description: Israel made a vow to the Lord and asked for victory over the Canaanites. They promised to devote the cities to complete destruction (cherem) if God handed their enemies over to them.

keyEvents.title: The Defeat of the Canaanites and Hormah
keyEvents.description: The Lord heard Israel's prayer and gave them victory over the Canaanites. The Israelites defeated them and completely destroyed their cities. The place was called Hormah, which means 'destruction' or 'ban'.

keyEvents.title: The King of Arad in Joshua's List of Conquered Kings
keyEvents.description: The king of Arad is listed among the Canaanite kings who were defeated during Joshua's conquest of the Promised Land.

keyEvents.title: Mention in Israel's Journey
keyEvents.description: In the summary of Israel's journey, it is mentioned that the Canaanite king of Arad, who lived in the Negev in the land of Canaan, heard that the Israelites were approaching.

versions.summary: Arad was a Canaanite king who ruled over the city of Arad in the Negev region south of Canaan. He attacked the Israelites as they approached Canaan and took some of them captive, but Israel made a vow to the Lord and ultimately defeated his people and destroyed their cities. Arad is also mentioned in connection with Joshua's conquest of Canaan.

versions.reason: [minor] The title is accurate and descriptive, but it should be clarified that 'Arad' here refers to the king of the city of Arad, not a person named 'Arad'. In the biblical text he is called 'the king of Arad' – Arad is the city name, not a personal name.; [major] The summary states that 'Arad is also mentioned in connection with Joshua's conquest of Canaan,' but it is important to clarify that this may refer to a different king of Arad than the one who attacked during the wilderness wanderings. It is unclear whether it is the same person. The summary should be formulated more precisely.; [major] Numbers 33:40 describes how the Canaanite king of Arad 'heard that the Israelites were coming.' This is a summarizing travel note, not necessarily a 'first confrontation' or a 'temporary setback'. Describing the event as a 'temporary setback' is misleading. Numbers 33:40 only mentions that the king of Arad lived in the Negev in the land of Canaan and heard that the Israelites were coming. It does not mention a defeat for Israel.; [minor] The dating 'c. 1400 BC' depends on which chronology one follows for the Exodus from Egypt (early dating c. 1446 BC vs. late dating c. 1260 BC). It may be more neutral to say 'Late 2nd millennium BC' or retain a broader formulation.; [minor] The role 'warrior' is reasonable based on his attack on Israel, but 'opponent of Israel' or 'enemy of Israel' could have been more descriptive of his biblical role.; [major] Footnotes are missing. Arad is an archaeologically very important site with extensive excavations (Tel Arad) that have uncovered both a Canaanite city and an Israelite fortress complex with a temple. Linguistic and historical details about the name and the place should also be mentioned.

When the Israelites approached Canaan, he attacked them and took some captive. Israel then made a vow to the Lord to utterly destroy his cities if God gave them victory. The Lord heard their prayer, and the Israelites defeated the Canaanites and completely destroyed their cities. The place was called Horma, which means 'devotion' or 'destruction'. A king of Arad is also listed among the defeated kings in Joshua's conquest list, though it is uncertain whether this is the same person.

However, the primary text in Numbers is correctly placed. No change needed.; [minor] The summary is good and theologically sound, but it could be strengthened by mentioning the Hebrew term 'cherem' (ban) more explicitly as a theological concept, as well as more clearly linking the event to the broader conquest narrative.; [minor] The description mentions 'cherem' in parentheses, which is helpful. footnotes.text: Tel Arad is one of the most thoroughly excavated archaeological sites in the Negev. The excavations have uncovered a large Canaanite city from the Early Bronze Age (ca. 2950–2650 B.C.) and an Israelite fortress from the Iron Age. Within the fortress, a small temple with an altar was discovered, offering unique insights into Israelite cultic practice outside Jerusalem. However, it is worth noting that the Canaanite city appears to have been abandoned for several hundred years before the arrival of the Israelites, which has led to discussions about whether the biblical king of Arad may have ruled over another nearby location.

The name 'Arad' (Hebrew: עֲרָד, 'Arad') may be related to the Hebrew word for 'wild donkey' (עָרוֹד), which could suggest a connection to the wildlife of the Negev desert. In the biblical text, Arad is primarily a place name, and 'the king of Arad' is a title rather than a personal name.

The place Horma (חָרְמָה), mentioned in Num 21:3, is derived from the Hebrew verb חרם (cherem) meaning 'to devote to destruction' or 'to ban'. This was a form of holy war where everything in a conquered city was devoted to God and destroyed. The practice reflects a theological understanding that God is the true owner of the spoils of war, and that complete destruction expresses total submission to His will.

There is scholarly discussion about the relationship between the events in Num 14:45, Num 21:1–3, and Judg 1:17. Some scholars believe that Horma received its name on more than one occasion, or that the various texts reflect different traditions related to the conquest of this area in the Negev.

In rabbinic tradition, the attack by the king of Arad is linked to the Israelites having lost the divine protection provided by the clouds (ananei hakavod) after Aaron's death (Num 33:40 is connected to Num 20:29). According to the Talmud (Rosh Hashana 3a), it was actually the Amalekites who attacked, disguised as Canaanites.
